claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 at.% silicon to a refractory high-entropy alloy promotes in-situ silicide formation.
The silicon addition promotes formation of a continuous protective SiO2 surface scale during extended high-temperature exposure in air.
The silicide and silica-scale formation significantly improves oxygen resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
A typical applicable refractory high-entropy alloy can be based on W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V.
The proposed beneficial effect should occur during exposure to air at approximately 1200°C for 10 hours.
In-situ-formed silicide particles develop a continuous SiO2 layer upon oxidation.
Silicon oxidizes preferentially within the alloy.
Silicide phases convert into a robust and adherent SiO2 scale at high temperature.
The SiO2 scale impedes oxygen ingress and slows oxidation of the underlying refractory phases.
The silicon-modified alloy will have a lower oxidation rate, thinner oxide scale, and lower oxidation-induced weight gain than the untreated alloy under identical conditions.
Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys typically develop thick oxide scales and high oxidation-induced weight gains in high-temperature air.
The silicon benefit may not manifest at lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing environments.
Interactions between silicon and other alloying elements may affect oxidation performance and long-term mechanical integrity.

contradictions.description: The structural-mediator field presents silicide particles as pre-existing intermediates that subsequently oxidize into silica, whereas the mechanism says that preferential silicon oxidation forms the silicide phases. This gives inconsistent formation order and chemistry for the proposed mediator.
